stem: The absolute diff erence between two treatments in a study is 6%. What is the NNT?
explanation: ABI-6% or 0.06. So NNT-1/0.06=16.666. NNT should be always corrected to the next highest number, and so the value is 17.

stem: What type of study design can be used tofi nd out the number of individuals with mental illness among those who are dependent on alcohol?
explanation: Cross-sectional surveys are studies aimed at determining the frequency (or level) of a particular attribute, such as a specifi c exposure, disease or any other health-related event, in a defi ned population at a particular point in time. For instance, we can carry out a cross- sectional survey to estimate the prevalence of hepatitis B infection, the prevalence of smoking or the pro- portion of women of childbearing age who are breast-feeding in a given population at the time of the survey (www.iarc.fr/en/publications/pdfs-online/epi/)

stem: Which of the following bias is controlled by allocation concealment?
explanation: Allocation concealment helps to reduce selection bias while blinding helps to reduce ascertainment bias.

stem: Which of the following is required when reporting the conduct and results of an RCT using thefl owchart recommended by the CONSORT guidelines?
explanation: CONSORT guidelines provide an updated checklist for adequate reporting of RCTs. CONSORT website (www.consort-statement.org) has helpful resources to improve reporting of randomised trials. Attrition rate must be always reported when drawing a CONSORTfl owchart.

stem: What will be the percentage of type 1 error if the results of a trial are precisely meeting the conventional level of signifi cance?
explanation: As p-value is conventionally 5%, there is 5 in 100 chances of type 1 error in a study.

stem: What's the purpose of concealment allocation?
options: Prevent subjective bias in reporting outcomes
correctAnswer: Prevent infl uencing group assignment in RCTs
explanation: Concealment allocation is a technique used to prevent selection bias by concealing the allocation sequence from those assigning participants to intervention groups, until the moment of the assignment. Allocation concealment prevents researchers from (unconsciously or otherwise) infl uencing which participants are assigned to a given intervention group.

stem: Which of the following clinical questions is better suited to qualitative rather than quantitative research methods?
options: A study to measure psychiatric symptoms after head injury
A study detailing the functional outcomes of people treated with Cognitive Behavioural Therapy
A study of the costs per unit of 'patient utility' in a randomized controlled trial
A study to measure quality of life in people with Alzheimer's disease.
A study to assess the attitudes of people with borderline personality disorder to their diagnosis
correctAnswer: A study to assess the attitudes of people with borderline personality disorder to their diagnosis
explanation: Qualitative research is often employed to understand the feelings, values, and perceptions that underlie and infl uence behaviour/health states.

stem: Which of the following conditions must be satisfi ed for odds ratio to come close or be the same as a relative risk?
options: If the odds ratio is in negative values
The prevalence of disease is relatively common
If the value of relative risk is 1
The prevalence of the disease is very low
If the value of odds ratio is more than 20
correctAnswer: The prevalence of the disease is very low
explanation: In case of disorders that have a low prevalence, odds ratio comes closer to relative risk.

stem: Which of the following data can provide a link between exposure to a risk factor and the disease studied?
explanation: Incidence rates are useful in epidemiological research for causality. Incidence rates can provide data on new cases developing after an exposure within a time period in a specifi ed population. Thus they are more useful than prevalence data to obtain a link between exposure and disease development.

stem: Which among the following provide the most powerful, useful evidence available and now attract a large citation rate?
explanation: Systematic reviews, because they provide the most powerful and useful evidence available, have become extremely important to clinicians and patients and now attract a massive citation rate (Tyrer 2008)

stem: Which of the following analysis converts outcomes into monetary units?
explanation: In cost-benefi t analysis, the inputs and outputs are both calculated in terms of monetary values.

stem: Which of the following best describes opportunity cost?
options: The capital cost of seeking a prospect e.g. an employment
ts of next best foregone alternatives when the available resources are utilised in one way
The extra costs associated with an expansion in the activity of an established service
The monetary loss due to an unprecedented opportunity.
ts of all other alternatives when the available resources are utilised in one way
correctAnswer: The benefi ts of next best foregone alternatives when the available resources are utilised in one way
explanation: Opportunity cost is defi ned as the benefi t that a resource would yield in its best alternative use. This is the benefi t forgone as a result of using the resource. Although, for practical purposes, the cost of a resource is generally expressed in money terms, in some cases there will be nofi nancial payment even though there is an opportunity cost e.g. a voluntary carer.

stem: Which of the following data requires the use of age-specifi c rates for its calculation?

In indirect age-adjustment, a common set of age-specifi c rates is applied to the populations whose rates are to be standardized.The simplest and most useful form of indirect adjustment is the standardized mortality ratio (SMR)": (Excerpt from: Naing, N. http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3406211/)

stem: Number of deaths of live infants (one year of age or younger) per 1000 live births is called
explanation: Deaths under 1 year of age expressed as a proportion of live births is an important public health index used by the UNICEF and the WHO. This is called infant mortality rate.

stem: Which of the following elements does not belong to the process of making treatment recommendations in the form of clinical guidelines?

ning the decision to be made

explanation: If guidelines are to achieve their potential, they should have adequate resources and be introduced through partnerships that may include clinicians, providers, purchasers and the public. stem: Which of the following factor is the least/not important in determining the quality of a meta-analysis?
options: Comparability of intervention among individual studies
Magnitude of outcome reported from individual studies
correctAnswer: Magnitude of outcome reported from individual studies
explanation: The ultimate quality of a meta-analysis depends on the quality of the primary studies on which it is based. A meta-analysis is most persuasive when data from a large number of methodologically rigorous randomized trials with large sample sizes are pooled, irrespective of the results reported in each trial.

stem: Which of the following graphs is primarily used to determine if there was a publication bias in your meta-analysis?

stem: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of narrative review but not systematic review?
options: literature search based on expert's familiarity
correctAnswer: literature search based on expert's familiarity
explanation: Narrative reviews generally are comprehensive and cover a wide range of issues within a given topic, but they do not necessarily state or follow rules about the search for evidence. Also, typical narrative reviews do not reveal how the decisions were made about the relevance of studies and the validity of the included studies. (from http://humupd.oxfordjournals.org/content/11/2/103.full)

explanation: Last three options do not measure central tendency.

stem: Which of the following is a parametric test?
explanation: Student's t-test is a parametric test; it is used to test if the means of observations from two samples are signifi cantly diff erent. Wilcoxon signed rank test is the non-parametric alternative to paired t-test. Mann-Whitney U test is the non-parametric alternative of the unpaired t test. Kruskal-Wallis test compares between the medians of two or more samples to determine if the samples have come from diff erent populations. It is a non-parametric equivalent of ANOVA while Friedman test is a non-parametric test analogous to repeated measures ANOVA.

stem: Which of the following is an agreed method of assessing quality of conducting and reporting systematic reviews and metaanalyses?
explanation: The Quality of Reporting of Meta-analyses (QUOROM) conference was convened to address standards for improving the quality of reporting of meta-analyses of clinical randomised controlled trials (RCTs). The QUOROM group consisted of 30 clinical epidemiologists, clinicians, statisticians, editors, and researchers. In conference, the group was asked to identify items they thought should be included in a checklist of standards. A modifi ed Delphi technique was used in assessing candidate items. The conference resulted in the QUOROM statement, a checklist, and afl ow diagram.

stem: Which of the following is an appropriate study design to compare two diff erent interventions with diff erent clinical outcomes in terms of monetary outcomes?
explanation: The cost-benefi t study compares two diff erent interventions with diff erent clinical outcomes. But in this case, all outcomes are translated into monetary (£££) terms and are then compared. This type of study is often preferred by managers to decide how to spend the allocated money eff ectively. Greenhalgh, T (2001). How to read a paper. BMJ Books, London.

stem: Which one among the following is a measure of internal consistency of a test?
explanation: Split-half reliability is a measure of internal consistency reliability. The items on the scale are divided into 2 halves and the resulting half scores are correlated in reliability analysis. High correlations between the halves indicate consistency in reliability analysis.

stem: The reduction in amount of disability in diagnosed patients is associated with
explanation: Tertiary prevention consists of prevention of disease progression and an attendant suff ering after it is clinically obvious and diagnosis is well established. This act also includes the rehabilitation of disabled conditions.

stem: The ability of a test to correctly classify subjects as being with or without a disease is called
explanation: This is the likelihood that a test result would be expected in patients with a condition, divided by the likelihood that that same result would be expected in patients without that condition. Imagine a blood test for anorexia, if the LR for a positive test is 5, it means if the test is positive in that patient, then that patient isfi ve times more likely to have anorexia than not have it.

stem: The term cost benefi t analysis refers to
options: Expressing all costs and consequences of an intervention in the same monetary units
Minimising both the costs and burdens associated with an intervention.
Expressing alternative interventions in cost per unit of health outcome
Comparing only the costs of two or more interventions
Examining the readiness to spend on an intervention
correctAnswer: Expressing all costs and consequences of an intervention in the same monetary units
explanation: It is an economic evaluation in which all costs and consequences of a program are expressed in the same units, usually money. It is used to determine allocative effi ciency; i.e., comparison of costs and benefi ts across programs serving diff erent patient groups.

stem: Which of the following is a possible outcome of early intervention in schizophrenia?
options: Reducing collateral psychosocial damage in critical period
explanation: The tenets of early intervention include reducing duration of untreated psychosis (DUP), promoting recovery fromfi rst episode of psychosis, minimising secondary morbidity and mortality, reducing collateral psychosocial damage in critical period, possibly neuroprotection, engagement with the patient at early stages facilitate longer treatment and reducing comorbidities such as substance use.

stem: Which of the following is the best examined antipsychotic in terms of negative symptoms of schizophrenia?
explanation: Negative symptoms include anhedonia, avolition, apathy, amotivation and restricted aff ect. SGAs were marketed as being especially effi cacious for negative symptoms; but evidence to support this hypothesis is scarce. Most RCTs are conducted on patients with predominantly positive symptoms. Amisulpride is still the best examined SGA as regards negative symptoms because several studies in patients with predominantly negative symptoms have been carried out with this compound. But the eff ect of amisulpiride in reducing negative symptoms at a low dose (50 to 100mg/day) may be due to concurrent reduction in positive symptoms or depression. When compared head to head with haloperidol, the eff ect of amisulpride on negative symptoms weakened.

stem: Which of the following is the most common comorbid illness in those with anorexia nervosa?
explanation: A lifetime prevalence of around 75% is seen for depression in those with anorexia.

stem: Which of the following is the most common feature of Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome?
explanation: The tetrad of NMS symptoms typically evolves over one to three days. In an analysis of 340 cases, 70 percent of patients followed a typical course of mental status changes appearingfi rst, followed by rigidity, then hyperthermia, and autonomic dysfunction (J Nerv Ment Dis. 1994;182(3):168.). Hyperthermia is a defi ning symptom according to many diagnostic criteria. Temperatures of more than 38ºC are typical (seen in upto 87% cases).

Lower doses of tricyclics can be used

explanation: If using a TCA for depression in HIV, most clinicians prefer secondary amines (eg, desipramine, nortriptyline) and reserve their use for patients with asymptomatic illness.AIDS patients can respond to lower dosages of tricyclics (25-100 mg), but they may also suff er severe anticholinergic eff ects at reduced dosages.

stem: Which of the following is true about pharmacological management of social phobia?
options: Antidepressants must be given at a higher dose than for depression
Antidepressants must be given at a lower dose than for depression
Antidepressants may take longer to work than for depression
Propranalol is useful in generalised subtype
correctAnswer: Antidepressants may take longer to work than for depression
explanation: The best established treatments are CBT and SSRIs. Paroxetine, sertraline,fl uoxetine andfl uvoxamine, escitalopram, venlafaxine have been evaluated in RCTs with favourable outcome. Normal antidepressant doses can be used but may need a longer 12 week trial to establish outcome. Drug treatment should continue for at least 6-12 months after response. Phenelzine is the second line treatment. Moclobemide is also eff ective.

stem: Which of the following is true about the diagnostic stability of personality disorders?

Most patients with borderline personality would meet criteria for the same at 10 years follow up.
A J shaped relationship exists between personality disorders and age
Cluster A becomes worse with age
correctAnswer: A J shaped relationship exists between personality disorders and age
explanation: For a long time it was thought that once diagnosed with personality disorder the diagnosis remains forever and no change takes place. This pessimism is now shifting largely due to long term follow-up studies in borderline personality. Results of epidemiological studies suggest a J- shaped relation between personality and age, with an initial decrease followed by an increase in some personality disorders in older people.

stem: Mr Y suff ered from post-stroke depression and was started on citalopram, on which he is showing a good response. What is the minimum duration he should stay on it?
explanation: National clinical guidelines for the management of mood disturbance after stroke (Intercollegiate Working group, 2004): Screen for depression and anxiety within thefi rst month of stroke , use standardized questionnaires for screening, Consider a trial of antidepressant medication in those with persistently depressed mood of at least 1 month's duration, If there is a good response, antidepressants should be continued for at least 6 months. Both Fluoxetine and Citalopram have RCT evidence to support their use, though Fluoxetine has not been consistently eff ective across trials.

stem: Which of the following is associated with narcolepsy?
explanation: Narcolepsy is associated with cataplexy (NOT catalepsy / waxyfl exibility – the latter are catatonic features). It is a disabling sleep disorder aff ecting 0·02% of adults worldwide. It is characterised by severe, irresistible daytime sleepiness and sudden loss of muscle tone (cataplexy), and can be associated with sleep-onset or sleep-off set paralysis and hallucinations, frequent movement and awakening during sleep, and weight gain. Sleep monitoring during night and day shows rapid sleep onset and abnormal, shortened rapid-eye-movement sleep latencies. The onset of narcolepsy with cataplexy is usually during teenage and young adulthood and persists throughout the lifetime. Pathophysiological studies have shown that the disease is caused by the early loss of neurons in the hypothalamus that produce hypocretin, a wakefulness-associated neurotransmitter present in cerebrospinalfl uid. The cause of neural loss could be autoimmune since most patients (>90%) have the HLA DQB1*0602 allele that predisposes individuals to the disorder. The frequency of HLA-DR2 is also increased in narcolepsy though not as high as HLA DQB1*0602. Treatment is with stimulant drugs to suppress daytime sleepiness, antidepressants for cataplexy, and ? hydroxybutyrate for both symptoms.

stem: Narcolepsy is characterized by all of the following except
explanation: Narcolepsy (from Dilley and Fleminger, 2006): Prevalence of 0.025% in the general population. Symptoms include excessive daytime sleepiness, sudden sleep attacks (narcolepsy) - the sleep is refreshing as it is REM in nature, cataplexy (seen in 75% of patients), sleep paralysis (seen in 30%), hypnagogic hallucinations. Only 10% of individuals present with all four phenomena. Automatic behaviours are reported in around one-third (complex behaviours that are not recalled when they regain alertness). The overall sleep duration per 24 hours is NOT increased in narcolepsy due to reduced and fragmented nocturnal sleep.

stem: Which of the following can be a preventative strategy to reduce the risk of schizophrenia across populations globally?
options: Preventing the emergence of clozapine resistance
cation of those at high risk
explanation: Mrazek and Haggerty (1994) framework for the prevention of mental disorders includes universal, selective and indicated prevention. Universal interventions are directed to a general population group. This is largely a primary prevention. Though these are directed at the general population who do not have specifi c risk factors, there are some epidemiological factors for schizophrenia that are so widespread that their targeting can be considered a universal intervention. E.g. urban living, poor social capital including low social cohesion, exclusion and discrimination, low socio-economic status, obstetric complications, illicit drug use, childhood trauma and experiencing stressful life events. Increasing social capital, decreasing discrimination, and reducing poverty are possible goals of universal prevention. But universal interventions are diffi cult to evaluate, costly, and need large scale implementation in diseases of low incidence such as schizophrenia. Early and eff ective interventions, rather than universal prevention strategies, are the most cost-eff ective population health strategies available. Selective approaches are targeted at people who are at increased risk based on an understanding of the known risk factors and/or aetiology of the disorder. Indicated approaches target high risk individuals with minimal but detectable signs or symptoms foreshadowing mental disorder, but who do not meet diagnostic levels currently. Both selective and indicated approaches are secondary prevention methods.

stem: Lucy is pregnant and is taking citalopram for her depression. What is the risk of her giving birth to a child with septal defects?
explanation: Mothers who took citalopram during pregnancy may have a 2-2.5 times greater risk of giving birth to a child with septal heart defects and a 6 times greater risk of giving birth to a child with Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension Newborn (PPHN). ). A large (n=493,113) population-based cohort study in Denmark found that the absolute increase in prevalence of septal heart defects was low with any SSRI (0.9% vs 0.5% amongst unexposed children). For specifi c SSRIs the prevalence of septal heart defects were 0.6% forfl uoxetine, 1.1% for citalopram and 1.5% for sertraline. It is unknown how many of these defects required surgery. (Pederson et al., BMJ 2009;339:b3569)

stem: Which of the following ethnic groups are more susceptible to dose-dependent side eff ects of risperidone?
explanation: Most East Asians lack one copy of fully functional CYP2D6 enzyme and so are intermediate metabolisers of risperidone. They develop more dose dependent side eff ects and require lower doses of risperidone.

stem: A patient has both schizophrenia-like and mania like aff ective symptoms concurrently during each relapse. He has been treated with various antipsychotics including olanzapine and quetiapine and is currently on haloperidol for last 12 weeks with minimal response. Which of the following is the best medication that can control his symptoms at this time?
explanation: Mood stabilizers are a mainstay of treatment for patients with schizoaff ective disorder. Carbamazepine is superior for schizoaff ective disorder, depressive type; lithium and carbamazepine have no diff erence in effi cacy for the manic schizoaff ective (bipolar like) disorder. Antipsychotics are often used as combination medications with mood stabilisers or primarily for mood stabilising eff ect itself.

stem: In Parkinson's related psychosis, hallucinations of which type of modality is common?
explanation: Parkinson's related Psychosis is mostly related to antiparinsonian drugs. Both dopaminergic/anticholinergic medications are implicated. Hallucinations are common, seen in 20% of cases- especially visual modality, delusions 3-30%. Low-dose (less than 100 mg/day) clozapine can improve psychosis without worsening parkinsonism. Quetiapine can also be used.

stem: Which one of the following is associated with a clinical picture of schizophrenia-like psychoses?
explanation: Paranoid schizophrenia-like symptoms occur in 6% to 25% of cases with Huntington's.

stem: Which of the following is associated with PANDAS?
explanation: Paediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorders associated with streptococcal infection - PANDAS is thought to be secondary to streptococcal infection and mediated by autoantibodies binding to basal ganglia. This produces tics,fl uctuating obsessive compulsive symptoms and anxiety.

stem: Which of the following medications can reduce plasma levels of Lamotrigine in a 34-year-old woman with bipolar disorder?
explanation: Oral contraceptives and carbamazepine can reduce Lamotrigine levels. Valproate can increase lamotrigine levels.

stem: At any given time, the proportion of general population (in percentage) who report sleep disturbances is
explanation: One third of otherwise normal people report insomnia. For most of these people, the problem is related to life style and habits.

stem: The functional neuroimagingfi nding seen in adult OCD is
options: Hypometabolism in the dominant parietal cortex
explanation: On the basis of an extensive review of functional neuroimaging studies, Saxena et al suggested that an imbalance of direct and indirect orbitofrontal-subcortical pathways mediates OCD symptoms. Recently, Adler et al reported that the change of OCD symptoms following a relapse is inversely correlated with the extent of activation in the left orbito-frontal cortex measured by functional MRI, suggesting the inhibitory role of left OFC in OCD symptom provocation.

stem: Myoclonic seizures have been reported with which of the following antipsychotic medication?
explanation: Olanzapine may aff ect EEG and Myoclonic seizures have been reported. Seizures rarely reported with Quetiapine but also shown to have anticonvulsant activity in ECT. Very limited data and clinical experience with Aripiprazole and seizures have been reported rarely. Ref: Maudsley prescribing guidelines, 10th edition; 337

stem: Oestrogen treatment in male to female (MTF) transsexuals produces all of the following bodily changes except
explanation: Oestrogen treatment in MTF transsexuals produces diminished libido and erectile function, some breast and hip development, and skin softening; there is no eff ect on voice pitch and speech therapy may be required to produce an acceptable female vocal pattern. Androgen treatment in FTM transsexuals produces muscle development, some lowering of vocal pitch, male pattern of bodily hair development, and amenorrhoea. Ref: Oxford handbook of psychiatry; 759

stem: OCD like symptoms may occur in patients with Huntington's disease due to the involvement of which area of the brain?
explanation: OCD like symptoms may occur due to basal ganglia involvement in patients with Huntington's disease.

stem: Which of the following statements is true of postnatal depression?
options: It occurs within 4-6 days of child birth
It is more likely in older mothers
It occurs in 10-15% of women after childbirth
It is more likely in women who have an assisted delivery
It is more likely in a woman from lower social class
correctAnswer: It occurs in 10-15% of women after childbirth
explanation: Postnatal depression is a signifi cant depressive episode, related to childbirth, occurring in 10-15% of women within 6 months post-partum (peak 3-4 weeks). Baby blues starts 2 -3 days after birth and lasts for one to two days. For postpartum psychosis, the peak occurrence is at 2 weeks postpartum.

stem: What is the most likely site of the primary tumour which when metastatic could cause symptoms of peripheral neuropathy and memory loss?
explanation: Presence of peripheral neuropathy along with memory loss as a result of malignant process could be due to pellagra. It is a rare presentation of carcinoid tumours that develop from neuroendocrine cells (mostly in the ileum) and produce serotonin. Generally 99% of body niacin is converted to nicotinic acid essential for cellular processes. In carcinoid syndrome, a huge fraction becomes spent on producing serotonin and bradykinins, leading to very low nicotininc acid availability. This causes the triad of dermatitis, diarrhea and dementia-like symptoms. An intestinal carcinoid does not usually produce the 'fl ush reaction' seen in carcinoid syndrome unless hepatic metastases have occurred, because metabolic products released by the tumour are rapidly destroyed by blood and liver enzymes in the portal circulation (eg, serotonin by hepatic monoamine oxidase).

stem: The following may make the diagnosis of hypomania diffi cult except:
explanation: Presence of elation may become apparent but in fact artefactual after recovery from depression. Substances with stimulant property, borderline personality with aff ective lability and ADHD can all individually mimic hypomania. Hypothyroidism is associated with lethargy and depressive features. In hyperthyroid state one may present as hypomanic or agitated depressed.

stem: Which one of the following factors indicates a higher risk of relapse of depression?
explanation: Presence of persistent dysthymia, comorbid conditions, including both psychiatric and general medical conditions, female gender, having longer episodes of illness before seeking treatment, greater number of prior episodes (3 or more;), being never married etc. Are some of the risk factors for relapse in depressive disorder.

stem: Premature ejaculation is a type of

stem: The rate of spontaneous congenital malformations associated with pregnancy is

stem: What is the most common presentation seen in women with postpartum psychosis?
explanation: Postpartum psychosis: An acute psychotic episode, occurring following 1.5/1000 live births, peak occurrence at 2 wks postpartum. Aetiology is unknown, but may relate to reduction of oestrogen (leading to DA super-sensitivity), cortisol levels, or postpartum thyroiditis. Symptoms 3 common clinical presentations: prominent aff ective symptoms (80%) mania or depression with psychotic symptoms; schizophreniform disorder (15%); acute organic psychosis (5%) Ref: Oxford handbook of psychiatry; 756

stem: A bipolar patient taking lithium was recently started on SSRI. Which of the following would you suspect as serotonin syndrome rather than lithium toxicity?

stem: Which one of the following is a positive prognostic factor for anorexia?
explanation: Younger age of onset is a positive prognostic factor for anorexia, in terms of short term outcome. The rest of the listed are negative prognostic factors.

stem: A family has recently moved near a countryside school. Their 6-year-old daughter does not speak to anyone at the school in thefi rst few months of enrolment. explanation: Selective mutism is seen in school age children presenting with refusal to speak in social settings such as a classroom. The language development may be normal. These children have a higher risk of later development of social phobia.

stem: A 40-year-old man has had 5 depressive episodes in the past and every time following treatment of depression he had developed hypomania. What would you prescribe?
explanation: Antidepressant-induced mania/hypomania has been reported with all major antidepressant classes in a subgroup of about 20-40% of bipolar patients. Lithium may confer better protection against this outcome when compared with other standard mood stabilizers, although switch rates have been reported with comparable frequencies on or off mood stabilizers. Mood switches were less frequent in patients receiving lithium (15%) than in patients not treated with lithium (44%) in a small naturalistic study. Risk factors for antidepressant induced switch includes (i) previous antidepressant-induced manias, (ii) a bipolar family history, and (iii) exposure to multiple antidepressant trials and (iv) initial illness beginning in adolescence or young adulthood. Henry C, Sorbara F, Lacoste J, Gindre C, Leboyer M. Antidepressant- induced mania in bipolar patients: identifi cation of risk factors. J Clin Psychiatry 2001 Apr;62(4):249-55

stem: What is the most appropriate treatment for a teenager with obsessive-compulsive disorder?
explanation: 1st line agents for OCD treatment are SSRIs (sertraline andfl uoxetine). Results from multiple randomised placebo-controlled trials of both medication and Cognitive-behavioural interventions in children and adolescents with OCD have confi rmed the most evidence for successful treatment of this disorder compared to any of the other anxiety disorders of childhood. A recent multi-site National Institute of Health funded investigation of Sertraline and cognitive-behavioural therapy each alone, and in combination for the treatment of childhood onset OCD, the Paediatric OCD Treatment Study (POTS) revealed that the combination was superior to either treatment alone. Sertraline also has UK license for OCD in teenagers.

stem: The rate of completed suicide in children and adolescents with bipolar disorder is
explanation: Early onset BPD has a poor outcome with 50% showing a long-term decline in function. The course is often chronic and less responsive to treatment, with atypical and rapid-cycling features especially diffi cult to treat. Suicide risk is high with rates of completed suicide approximately 10%.

stem: What percentage of children with major depressive episode will later manifest bipolar disorder?
explanation: About 20% of children and adolescents who initially show serious depression will "switch" to manic or mixed (manic-depressive) episodes.

stem: A man with Parkinson's disease develops psychotic symptoms. He has never been on antipsychotics before. The best treatment for him is:
explanation: Clozapine is the most eff ective drug for psychosis in Parkinson's disease. But the practical limitations of its use have led to trials of other atypical antipsychotics that do not require the intensive monitoring that is necessary for clozapine. Of these, quetiapine shows the most promise, but placebo-controlled trials are lacking. The use of olanzapine, risperidone and aripiprazole appears limited by unacceptable motor deterioration (Samuel et al.2006). Excerpt from Samuel et al. Clinical management of Parkinson's disease dementia: pitfalls and progress. Advan. Psychiatr. Treat. Mar 2006; 12: 121 - 129.

stem: Which antidementia drug inhibits both acetylcholinesterase and Butyl cholinesterase in the CNS?
explanation: Donepezil (Aricept), rivastigmine (Exelon), Galantamine (Reminyl) are cholinesterase inhibitors used to treat mild to moderate cognitive impairment in Alzheimer's disease. These drugs can be used in patients with MMSE score between 10 and 20. They act by decreasing the inactivation Acetylcholine and, thus, potentiating the cholinergic neurotransmission. This can lead to some (but not long lasting) improvement in memory and goal-directed thought. Donepezil is well tolerated and widely used. Rivastigmine (inhibits both acetyl and butyrylcholinesterases) and Galantamine appear more likely to cause gastrointestinal (GI) and neuropsychiatric adverse eff ects than does Donepezil. These medications cannot prevent the progressive neuronal degeneration seen in the disorder. Tacrine is rarely used, because of its potential for hepatotoxicity. Memantine (Ebixa) protects neurons from excessive amounts of glutamate, which may be neurotoxic. Trials show benefi ts of Memantine augmentation of Donepezil. Cochrane review indicates use in DAT, vascular and mixed dementias.

stem: Mr. Y suff ers from a long-standing diagnosis of Parkinson's disease and has developed a related dementia. Which of the following drugs has trial support for effi cacy?
explanation: Rivastigmine has good evidence for treatment of Parkinson's dementia and Lewy body dementia.

stem: What is the SECOND most common cause of dementia in the under 65s?
explanation: Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia in younger people. Around one-third of younger people with dementia have Alzheimer's disease. Vascular dementia is the second most common form of dementia in younger people. Around 20 per cent of younger people with dementia have vascular dementia. Around 12 per cent of younger people with dementia have frontotemporal dementia (data from alzheimers.org.uk).

stem: What percentage of patients with learning disability suff ers from a severe form of mental retardation?
explanation: Mild mental retardation (IQ range, 50 to 70) represents approximately 85 percent of persons with mental retardation. Moderate mental retardation (IQ range, 35-50) represents about 10 percent of persons with mental retardation. Severe mental retardation (IQ range, 20-35) comprises about 4 percent of individuals with mental retardation. Profound mental retardation (IQ range below 20) constitutes approximately 1 to 2 percent of persons with mental retardation. Most individuals with profound mental retardation have identifi able causes for their condition.

stem: What is the most common behavioural phenotype seen in Prader-Willi syndrome?
options: Increased appetite and incessant skin picking
correctAnswer: Increased appetite and incessant skin picking
explanation: Behavioural phenotypes: Food obsession, insatiable appetite, hyperphagia, obesity, skin picking are all important behavioral phenotypes seen in Prader-Willi syndrome.

stem: What is the prevalence of depression among individuals with intellectual disabilities?
explanation: The prevalence of depression is around 2-4%. Depressed mood and vegetative symptoms are the most striking symptoms, even though complaints of depression are not always expressed. A depressive mood is not verbalized, particularly among individuals at a lower intelligence level, but may well be observable.

stem: 'Hypertelorism' is a feature seen in which of the following conditions?
explanation: Hypertelorism refers to an abnormally increased distance between two organs or bodily parts, usually referring to an increased distance between the orbits (eyes). It is seen in some conditions like Di George's syndrome, Noonan syndrome, Edwards syndrome, cridu-chat syndrome and neurofi bromatosis. Salient features of DiGeorge syndrome can be summarized using the mnemonic CATCH-22, with the 22 reminding us of chromosome 22, andCATCH referring to Cardiac Abnormality, Abnormal facies (palatal abnormalities, hypertelorism), Thymic aplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia/Hypoparathyroidism.

stem: A woman was said to employ repeatedly a "neurotic defense mechanism". Which of the following is likely to be observed?
explanation: Converting unconscious impulses into their opposites, resulting in behaviour that is completely the opposite of what one feels, is called reaction formation. It can work eff ectively for coping in the short term, but on repeated use, will produce signifi cant 'neurotic' symptoms.

stem: Which of the following statements best describes the therapeutic technique of shaping?
options: Removing all sources of information for an allotted time
c appropriate behaviours while ignoring inappropriate behaviours
Repeated demonstration of the behaviour required
Reinforcing gradual approximations of a behaviour
Removal of previously earned reinforcers as a consequence of negative behaviour
correctAnswer: Reinforcing gradual approximations of a behaviour
explanation: Shaping: This is a form of operant conditioning where a desirable behaviour pattern is learnt by the successive reinforcement of behaviours closer to the desired one. This is used in training animals in circus where the dog is reinforced when it runs towards the circle, then when it jumps near the circle, then when it jumps through the circle and at last when it jumps through the circle offi re. This is also called successive approximation.

stem: Most patients engage in certain subtle behaviours while in a fearful situation that serve to maintain the fear. These behaviours are called
explanation: In-situation safety behaviours (Salkovskis) refer to a variety of subtle behaviours/internal mental processes that most patients engage in while in a fearful situation. These are intended to prevent feared outcome e.g., a panic disorder patient bows his head down and gently leans leftwards when having a panic, with a hope to increase heart's circulation.

stem: Which of the following statement is true with respect to the evidence on routine screening for dementia for all patients in primary care settings?
options: Screening is found to be eff
Screening is clearly harmful when off
ered to elderly with no complaints
Screening is the only way of reducing the public health impact of dementia
Screening is not useful as the available tests have low sensitivity though high specifi
cient evidence in primary care attendees
correctAnswer: Screening for dementia has insuffi cient evidence in primary care attendees
explanation: The United States Preventive Services Task Force systematically reviewed the evidence and concluded that the evidence is insuffi cient to recommend for or against routine screening for dementia in older adults in primary care. The task force found good evidence that some screening tests have good sensitivity but only fair specifi city in detecting cognitive impairment and dementia. There is fair to good evidence that several drug therapies have a benefi cial eff ect on cognitive function, but the evidence of their benefi cial eff ects on activities of daily living is mixed, with the benefi t being small at best. There is insuffi cient evidence to determine whether the benefi ts observed in drug trials are generalizable to patients whose disease would be detected by screening in primary care settings. The accuracy of diagnosis, the feasibility of screening and treatment in routine clinical practice, and the potential harms of screening (for example, labeling eff ects) are also unknown. The task force, therefore, could not determine whether the benefi ts of screening for dementia outweigh the harms. NICE has no recommendations for screening though it advises on early recognition and referral. (Retrieved from http://annals.org/article.aspx? articleid=716466)

stem: Aggression turned inward' could be a psychodynamic explanation for
explanation: Aggression turned inwards cause suicidal ideas and depression. When exhibited outwards, acting out' and violent, impulsive acts result.

stem: In psychotherapy, containment is best described as
options: The ability of the therapist to distract the patient from distressing re-enactments
The ability of the therapist to modify and return to the patient the diffi
cult material in a way he can tolerate.
The ability of therapist to keep the information given to him in a confi
The capacity of the therapist to withhold the emotional content during therapeutic sessions
The capacity of the therapist to appreciate the object relationships emerging during the therapy
correctAnswer: The ability of the therapist to modify and return to the patient the diffi cult material in a way he can tolerate.
explanation: The capacity of the psychotherapist to act similar to an emotionally competent mother who interacts with her infant was termed as Alpha function by Bion. Similiar to the mother, the alpha function allows the therapist to metabolise unbearable feelings on behalf of the patient. These are then fed back to the patient in a form that is easy for the patient to assimilate and link with his thoughts. This process is called containment in Bion's original sense. But later this term expanded variably, rather inaccurately referring to a capacity to hold all kinds of anxieties on a patient's behalf. P950: Puri and Treasaden: Psychiatry: An Evidence-based text

stem: Tom is on methadone treatment for heroin addiction. He attends A& E on two occasions saying he is running out of a supply of methadone and demanding treatment. What is the best course of action?
explanation: It is possible that he is experiencing withdrawal symptoms, due to an inadequate dose of methadone and possibly self-medicating himself. The best course of action is to stabilise this patient by optimizing the dose of methadone. It is inadvisable to issue additional replacement opiates from the A&E Department. Liaising and passing on this information to the local drug service is what is essential so that they can review their prescribing and possibly increase the daily dose with closer supervision.

stem: Which of the following is a projective test of personality?
explanation: Murray was the proponent of projective personality tests though thefi rst test produced was Rorschach's ink blots. Thematic Apperception Test (Murray), Draw-a-person test, sentence completion tests are other examples.

stem: Massed practice can be used in the treatment of;
explanation: Massed negative practice is one of the most frequently used behavioral techniques in the treatment for tic disorder. The patient is asked to deliberately perform the tic movement for specifi ed periods of time interspersed with brief periods of rest.

stem: Sally is physically dependent on dihydrocodeine, which she is taking for back pain. She wants to stop and go back to work. What is the best course of action?
explanation: Withdraw codeine cautiously in thefi rst instance, in conjunction with other pain management approaches (e.g., pregabalin, SNRI, psychology, TENS) and if unsuccessful then consider changing to methadone to facilitate withdrawal.

stem: Tim is taking heroin regularly. He has been tried unsuccessfully on methadone and buprenorphine. Choose next best option;
explanation: The guidelines suggest that the patient should have "specifi cally optimised higher dose oral methadone or buprenorphine maintenance treatment" after oral maintenance therapy before moving on to injectables. Injectable heroin and methadone treatments should be considered only for the minority of patients who are genuinely unresponsive to an optimised oral maintenance treatment approach. Injectable and oral substitute prescribing must be supported by locally commissioned and provided mechanisms for supervised consumption. Injectable drugs may present more risk of overdose than oral preparations and have a greater value on illicit markets and hence may require greater levels of supervision.(Retrieved from:www.nta.nhs.uk/uploads/nta_injectable_heroin_and_methadone_2003_fullguide.pdf)

stem: A man who repeatedly presents to A& E with his girlfriend who is pregnant and heavy abuser of heroin. She plans to breastfeed following childbirth. Which medication is preferable to continue if she starts breastfeeding
explanation: Methadone is considered compatible with breast-feeding. The Clinical Guidelines recommend that breast feeding should still be encouraged, but that with regards to methadone and breast feeding "the dose is kept as low as possible while maintaining stability, and the infant monitored to avoid sedation. (Ref: The Maudsley prescribing guidelines- 316)

stem: Which of the following drugs used to prevent relapse in alcohol use appears to act centrally on glutamate and GABA neurotransmitter system?
explanation: Acamprosate is a synthetic taurine analogue, which appears to act centrally on glutamate and GABA neurotransmitter system. It is licensed to prevent relapse in alcohol use and has been found to have a modest treatment eff ect.

stem: Mr Y was admitted to the orthopaedic ward three days ago after sustaining a fracture to his right femur following a road traffi c accident. He became confused, distracted and agitated in the next 2-3 days following surgery. His blood and urine tests are normal. The most likely diagnosis is;
explanation: Delirium tremens is a toxic confusional state that occurs when alcohol withdrawal symptoms are severe. The symptoms typically peak between 72-96 hours after the last drink. The classical symptoms include confusion, distraction & clouding of consciousness, vivid hallucinations aff ecting every sensory modality and marked tremors. Clinical features also includefl eeting paranoid delusions, agitation, sleep disturbances, signs of autonomic hyperactivity such as fever, sweating, tachycardia and hypertension

stem: Following sudden cessation of alcohol on a dependent patient, the risk of seizure is high during?
explanation: As part of alcohol withdrawal symptoms, generalized seizures rarely occur, usually within 24 hours of cessation of alcohol. Benzodiazepines especially long-acting ones such as diazepam reduce the risk of seizures.

stem: A man after completing his opioid detoxifi cation is highly motivated to remain on treatment and wants advice about maintaining it. Which of the following drugs is best suited in this situation?
explanation: Naltrexone is recommended as a treatment option in detoxifi ed, formerly opioid-dependent subjects who are highly motivated to remain in an abstinence programme. For this group, naltrexone treatment has been found by NICE to be a cost eff ective treatment strategy in aiding abstinence from opioid misuse. (www.nice.org.uk- Technology Appraisal 115, 2007)

stem: The MacArthur Competence Assessment Tool for Treatment (MacCat-T) includes assessment of all of the following except
explanation: The MacCat-T is the product of an 8-year study of patients' capacities to make treatment decisions. It is a semi-structured interview that assists clinicians who are conducting assessments of patients' competence to consent to treatment. It takes 20-25mins to administer and tests the following: Understanding disorder and treatment proposed, appreciation of treatment and disorder, understanding benefi ts and risk,fi rst choice and reasoning, alternative choices, generating consequences andfi nal choice. Thefi nal score is given in four areas: understanding, appreciation, expressing a choice, and reasoning.

stem: The prevalence of antisocial personality among females prisoners in the UK is
explanation: Surveys of prisoners worldwide indicate a prevalence of antisocial personality disorder of 47% for men and 21% for women (Fazel & Danesh, 2002). In the UK prison population, the prevalence of people with antisocial personality disorder has been identifi ed as 63% male remand prisoners, 49% male sentenced prisoners, and 31% female prisoners (Singleton et al., 1998). By contrast, the prevalence of psychopathy in UK prisoners is only 4.5% using a PCL-R score of >30, and 13% using a score of >25 (Hare et al., 2000).

stem: What proportion of off enders commit nearly 50% of all reported crime?
explanation: Repeat Off enders: In Wolfgang's famous Philadelphia cohort, about 5 percent of all off enders in the study were responsible for more than 50 percent of the crimes. Similarly, according to the British Crime Survey, repeat victims (just over 4 percent of all victims) endure 40 percent of the crimes reported in the survey.

stem: You are asked to write a court report for a man convicted of a sexual assault. Which of the following is most likely to increase his risk of further off ending?
options: Two previous charges for sexual violence
correctAnswer: Two previous charges for sexual violence
explanation: A Higher number of sex off ences and Previous criminal history are important risk factors to increase the risk of further sexual violence in someone who has been charged with a sexual off ence.

stem: Epidemiological terms I Choose one answer from the given list for each option below Ratio between deaths due to a specifi c cause and total number of deaths in a population Ratio between number of deaths due to all cause in a population and total population size Ratio between number of deaths due to a specifi c disease and number of persons aff ected by the disease in a population A health gap measure that includes premature mortality equivalent years of 'healthy' life lost due to disease state Choose... Choose... Choose... Choose...
correctAnswer:
Ratio between deaths due to a specifi c cause and total number of deaths in a population → Proportionate mortality rate, Ratio between number of deaths due to all cause in a population and total population size → Crude mortality rate, Ratio between

number of deaths due to a specifi c disease and number of persons aff ected by the disease in a population → Case fatality rate, A health gap measure that includes premature mortality equivalent years of 'healthy' life lost due to disease state → Disability adjusted life years
explanation: Description 1fi ts proportionate mortality rate: It is a measure of contribution of a disease to societal mortality burden. Description 2fi ts crude mortality rate: A crude rate is any rate applicable to whole population. Case fatality rate (decription 3) is a measure of the fatal severity of the disease studied. For example, 15 patients out of 100 with anorexia will die due to its complications. The DALY (description 4) is a health gap measure that extends the concept of potential years of life lost due to premature death (PYLL) to include equivalent years of 'healthy' life lost in states of less than full health, broadly termed disability.

Suicide by occupation Random eff ects meta-analyses were conducted to calculate a pooled risk of suicide across various occupational skill-level groups across working-age adults (Milner et al. Suicide by occupation:systematic review and meta-analysis. The British Journal of Psychiatry Dec 2013, 203 (6) 409-416). Thirty-four studies were included in the meta-analysis. Occupational grouping was assigned using major codes from the International Standard Classifi cation of Occupations (ISCO) (version 2008). These were: ISCO 1 (managers, senior offi cials and legislators), ISCO 2 (professionals), ISCO 3 (technicians and associate professionals), ISCO 4 (clerks), ISCO 5 (service and sales workers), ISCO 6 (skilled agricultural andfi shery workers), ISCO 7 (craft and related trades workers), ISCO 8 (plant and machine operators, and assemblers), and ISCO 9 (elementary occupations). Results suggested a stepwise gradient in risk, with the lowest skilled occupations being at greater risk of suicide than the highest skill-level group. A forest plot with the risk ratios for each subgroup is shown below. Using the information displayed, choose the most appropriate responses for the questions that follow.

1. The occupational groups showing NO signifi cant association with suicide risk (Choose THREE):

2. The occupational groups with the highest risk of suicide (Choose TWO):

3. The occupational group with the lowest risk of suicide (Choose ONE) 4. The occupational group with the lowest number of studies included in the subgroup analysis (Choose ONE) 5. The occupational group with the most precise estimate of the level of association in this analysis (Choose ONE) 6. The occupational group with studies showing the highest degree of heterogeneity (Choose ONE): 1. Two groups - ISCO 2 and 3, have confi dence intervals of risk estimates that cross the line of no eff ect (RR=1).In the case of ISCO 7, the confi dence intervals 'touch' the line - or include the value 1 (as the range is given as 1.0 to 1.3). This is also not a signifi cant result. 2. The highest risk of suicide is notable for the ISCO category 9, (RR = 1.8, 95% CI 1.5-2.3) and the ISCO category 8 group, (RR = 1.8, 95% CI 1.2-2.6). 3. The lowest risk of suicide was seen for the ISCO category 1, (RR = 0.7, 95% CI 0.50-0.9) 4. Note that this forest plot is not a display of individual studies included in the analysis; instead, it only shows the summary results of studies in each of the diff erent occupational subgroups. The number of studies included in each subgroup can be ascertained from the degrees of freedom. The lowest value of 7 corresponds to ISCO 1. 5. The precision of the estimate can be ascertained from the width of the reported confi dence intervals or alternatively, by inspecting the length of the horizontal lines across each blob. ISCO 7 has the shortest line, and thus the most precise set of results. 6. The heterogeneity of the results in each subgroup (or more precisely, the impact of this heterogeneity on the overall results) can be ascertained from the I value presented in thefi gure. I value provides the percentage of the variability in eff ect estimates that is due 2 2

to heterogeneity rather than due to a chance observation. Values of I from 75% to 100% indicate considerable heterogeneity. The highest value in this plot is 99.6, which corresponds to ISCO category 6. (Ref: http://handbook.cochrane.org/chapter_9/9_5_2_identifying_and_measuring_heterogeneity.htm) The correct answer is: 1. ISCO 2,3 and 7 2. ISCO 8 and 9 3. ISCO1 4. ISCO1 5. ISCO 7 6. ISCO 6 2
correctAnswer: 1. ISCO 2,3 and 7 2. ISCO 8 and 9 3. ISCO1 4. ISCO1 5. ISCO 7 6. ISCO 6 2

Personality disorders (3) From the descriptions given below, choose the type of personality disorder that is being referred to: Emotional instability, unclear self-image, chronic feelings of emptiness, intense, unstable relationships. Eccentric appearance with odd behaviour, vague circumstantial odd speech, odd beliefs with magical thinking and transient quasi-psychotic episodes. Callous unconcern for others, gross and persistent irresponsibility, low tolerance of frustration, lacks remorse. Persistent feelings of tension, belief that one is inferior to others, avoids activities where one might be criticized or rejected Choose... Choose... Choose... Choose...
correctAnswer: Emotional instability, unclear self-image, chronic feelings of emptiness, intense, unstable relationships. → Borderline, Eccentric appearance with odd behaviour, vague circumstantial odd speech, odd beliefs with magical thinking and transient quasi-psychotic episodes. → Schizotypal, Callous unconcern for others, gross and persistent irresponsibility, low tolerance of frustration, lacks remorse. → Dissocial, Persistent feelings of tension, belief that one is inferior to others, avoids activities where one might be criticized or rejected → Anxious
explanation:
Patients with borderline personality disorder have poor self-image, unstable personal relationships, impulsive behaviour in areas such as personal safety and substance misuse, may self-harm, feel suicidal and act on these feelings, experience instability of mood, and often have episodes of micro-psychosis. Feelings of chronic emptiness and fears of abandonment - termed as rejection sensitivity may lead to formation of multiple intense but short lasting relations. Patients with schizotypal personality disorder (in ICD10 this is classifi ed as a type of schizophrenia) appear odd or eccentric, may have illusions and magical thinking, obsessions without resistance, may be members of quasi-cultural groups, thought disorders and paranoia, may have transient psychotic features.

Patients with antisocial (or dissocial) personality disorder show a lack of regard for the rights and feelings of other people, lack of remorse for actions that may hurt others, ignore social norms about acceptable behaviour, may disregard rules and break the law, make relations easily but break them equally easily and a small proportion may be psychopathic. Patients with avoidant (anxious) personality disorder often fear being judged negatively by other people, hold feelings of discomfort in group or social settings, may come across as being socially withdrawn, have low self-esteem, and believe that they are inferior to others, may crave aff ection but fear rejection.

Childhood and developmental disorders (4) Choose the correct diagnosis for each of the following situations An 8-year-old girl is restless, not sleeping well and has frequent stomach aches. She is also missing school frequently A 7-year-old girl cannot speak at the school when called upon by teachers. However, she whispers in her friend's ear to communicate with her A 7-year-old girl is attending a ballet dance class in her school. However, she is extremely fearful to perform in front of others at the dance class as "it would be an embarrassment". As a result, she is missing her classes frequently. A 10-year-old boy was caught in afi re accident four months ago. He has diffi culty going to sleep, recurrent recollections of the event and has nightmares. He has poor concentration, and there is a decline in his school academic performance. Choose... Choose... Choose... Choose...
correctAnswer: An 8-year-old girl is restless, not sleeping well and has frequent stomach aches. She is also missing school frequently → Generalised anxiety disorder, A 7-year-old girl cannot speak at the school when called upon by teachers. However, she whispers in her friend's ear to communicate with her → Selective mutism, A 7-year-old girl is attending a ballet dance class in her school. However, she is extremely fearful to perform in front of others at the dance class as "it would be an embarrassment". As a result, she is missing her classes frequently. → Social phobia, A 10-year-old boy was caught in afi re accident four months ago. He has diffi culty going to sleep, recurrent recollections of the event and has nightmares. He has poor concentration, and there is a decline in his school academic performance. → PTSD
explanation:
1) The diagnosis is generalized anxiety disorder. The symptoms in children include somatic symptoms (such as headache, stomach pains, rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath), nail biting, hair pulling and school refusal. 2) The diagnosis is selective mutism that is a disorder characterized by a persistent failure to speak in specifi c settings (school) despite full use of language at home or with family. It may be found in younger children with social phobia. A child with selective mutism may remain completely silent or near silent, in some cases whispering instead of speaking out loud.

3) The diagnosis is the social phobia, which is characterized by marked fear of one or more social, or performance-related situations where the person is exposed to scrutiny and in which embarrassment may occur. Exposure to such social situations usually causes an anxiety reaction that is recognized as inappropriate. Therefore, such situations are either avoided or endured with discomfort. In severe cases, it may lead to school refusal in children. 4) Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterized by a set of symptoms such as intrusive thoughts about a traumatic event, persistent avoidance, and hyperarousal (poor sleep, poor concentration leading to decline in performance at school) in response to exposure to one or more traumatic events. Unlike most anxiety disorders, PTSD involves reactions to memories of past events rather than the anticipation of impending threat.
